title: The Ford GT70 Is a Mid-Engine Rally Hero That Never Quite Made the Podium

body_markdown:
You’ve read the headline, so you know where this is headed, but we bet you’d have had trouble guessing the car based on its recipe alone: a two-seater with a composite body, a mid-mounted, small-displacement V-6, and built specifically to take on the World Rally Championship. Did you go with the Lancia Stratos? Well, no. In this case, it’s actually a long-forgotten Ford.


Say hello to the Ford GT70, a super-lightweight homologation special that combined British engineering, Italian design, and race-winning mechanicals. Was it successful? No, it was not. There’s a reason you’ve never heard of this thing, and it’s mostly because it didn’t get the job done while rally-spec versions of the Ford Escort did.


Consider what could have been: With a little more development, the GT70 might well have been a credible rival to the Stratos’ WRC hat trick in the mid-1970s. And, in the context of one of Ford’s greatest European motorsport machines—the RS200 of the wild Group B days—the GT70 could have become a truly interesting and collectible road car in homologation form.


Mechanics prepare the Ford GT70 of Guy Chasseuil and Christian Baron during the Corsica Rally on November 3, 1972.


LAT Images/Getty Images


It never quite made it that far, but unlike some of Ford’s other[abandoned mid-engined dreams](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/mid-engine-mustang/) , the GT70 did actually race. Five hundred customer cars were planned for, but only six were built. The effort started strong, and Ford was serious enough about it to put Len Bailey on the case. Chief executive engineer on the Le Mans–winning GT40 program, Bailey later had a hand in several successful Can-Am and other racing chassis over the years, and he had the chops to turn the GT70 into something great.


Ford


The issue, as ever, was money. Anyone who’s studied the history of the Ford GT40 will know that the early days of that project were anything but smooth, and making the car a winner took an immense amount of work at great expense. Ford’s European operations didn’t have that kind of wallop to get the GT70 properly sorted to take on works-prepped Porsche 911s and Alpine A110s, so when success didn’t come easy, the effort was dropped.


Still, even as a footnote of Ford history, the GT70 is an interesting blip on the radar. The audacity of the plan was respected enough that Ford still keeps at least one restored example around for occasional shows.


## Middle Management


Ford


Engineers have long understood the advantages (and drawbacks) of putting a car’s engine in the middle, and the layout began to prove itself in the 1960s, both on track and in production sports cars. Ford did more than dabble with this layout with the GT40, and it also built multiple mid-engined Mustang prototypes, including the Mustang I roadster, the Mach 2A, and the slightly ridiculous Low Investment Drivetrain (LID) Mustang, which had a 429-cubic-inch V-8 where the rear seats should be.


Ford


With all of this optimistic engineering sloshing around, and the example of the Alpine A110 proving that a then-unconventional layout in a rally car could be properly quick, it’s little wonder Ford decided to go mid-engined for the GT70. In fact, the Ford folks formed their plan on the very flight back from the 1970 Monte Carlo Rally, where the podium had been Porsche 911, Porsche 911, Alpine A110.


The featherweight Alpines had nowhere near the punch of the Porsches but might well have won that year had not the relatively snow-free conditions favored competitors with a little more available horsepower. The Alpines would go on to sweep the top three spots in 1971.


Ford team principal Stuart Turner and his Ford GT70 during the Rally Monte Carlo on January 22, 1971.


LAT Images/Getty Images


To Ford competition director Stuart Turner and racer Roger Clark, the solution was simple. Lightweight construction plus a punchy V-6, and *Bob’s your uncle* , as the Brits say. By the time they landed back in the U.K., plans were afoot.


It took a gestation of just nine months to go from that in-flight discussion to some real-deal prototypes, midwifed along by the aforementioned Len Bailey. Now a freelance designer, he sketched out a lightweight frame that would accept a 2.6-liter Cologne V-6, mounted to a five-speed manual transaxle. The fiberglass body was drawn up by Ercole Spada of Zagato, and on paper at least, things looked promising.


Ford


Ford


Factory tune on a Cologne engine from that era was a not-bad 120 horsepower or so, but it got bumped up to a solid 150 hp in the later Capri RS2600. In competition trim in the GT70, it made as much as 240 hp, which was plenty to get its 1700-pound chassis down the road. Top speed was estimated at around 180 mph, although that may well be optimistic engineering.


Ford


Video footage exists of Clark sliding the prototype GT70 around a field during shakedown testing, and the car looks and sounds pretty impressive. It slightly resembles an Opel GT, and the pop-up headlights jiggle over the bumps, but it slides smoothly, and the V-6 sounds great. The interior is also basically finished to what could be the level of a production car.


## A Thoroughbred and a Scrapper


While the genesis of the GT70 was the Ford Escort’s poor showing at the 1970 Monte Carlo rally, it’s worth noting that the Escort had immediately made a comeback at that year’s Finnish 1000 Lakes rally. Ford’s Turner noted that the Escort is a proven touring car champion and excelled in rough conditions. Winning in rallies was also great PR for an ordinary family car, as it emphasized to the public how tough the Escort was.


Flickr/IFHP97


The GT70, on the other hand, was more in the vein of the original GT40 effort: Victory here would burnish Ford’s engineering credentials rather than highlight the ruggedness of a production car sold to the public. With the higher-speed sections of the European rally circuit in the crosshairs, the GT70’s development separated from the Escort’s mission statement, where light and fast trumped durability.


Here’s where the wheels come off slightly, however. At first, rigidity was an issue, as the GT70 was plenty light but not stiff enough. The V-6 also proved to be slightly too tall, and there were a host of mechanical issues with suspension and braking. In rally, success comes with breaking parts and then making refinements back at the workshop, and that takes time and money.


LAT Images/Getty Images


Following a mediocre showing at a couple of races in 1971, the GT70’s real issue was a lack of both of those things. Even as it was struggling through teething issues, the Escort continued to prove it was a winning formula, even against more exotic layouts. Add in the rally-on-Sunday, sell-on-Monday appeal of having Escorts atop the podium, and Ford decided the money allocated to the GT70 would be better spent elsewhere.


Before shutting off the spigot, though, Ford France fitted a GT70 with a 1.6-liter Cosworth four-cylinder and turned the car into more of an Alpine A110 rival. It was much quicker and nimbler, but would have needed refinement to be properly competitive. Ford pulled the plug in 1973, packed away this GT70, and there the story draws toward its conclusion.


LAT Images/Getty Images


As a postscript, Ford pulled a modified GT70 out of mothballs in 2002, fitted a 200-hp 2.0-liter Cosworth BDA engine, and properly restored the rest of the car. Preserved by Ford Heritage, the example you see at the top of the page has run up the hill at the Goodwood Festival of Speed, and it preserves the spirit of the short run of six cars.


Eventually, Ford would get its mid-engined rally hero with the RS200, and the GT70 can be thought of as the grandfather of that car. Though it never achieved the status of Ford’s best-loved GT car, the GT70 was not just a dead-end footnote, but a foreshadowing of rally success.


Ford
